issues.legal_issue: A fishing arrangement limited to the fish caught from a tank, without rights in its subsoil or banks, does not establish a lease of the tank for purposes of the statutory vesting of a tank fishery.
material_facts: The tank was recorded as the absolute debuttar property of a deity, and its income and usufruct supported the deity’s maintenance and worship.
A revisional record and a receipt described two persons as tenants under a nine-year lease at an annual rent, but there was no deed or other document evidencing the alleged lease.

The alleged occupants acquired no rights in the tank’s subsoil or embankments; their interest was limited to fish they caught, in return for payment and an obligation to cleanse and maintain the tank.
The State claimed that the alleged lease made the occupants, rather than the deity, direct tenants of the State after vesting.
issues.conclusion: The arrangement was a licence to fish, not a lease of the tank. The deity, through its shebaits, was entitled to hold the tank fishery directly under the State; the alleged fishers did not become direct tenants of the State.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 6(1)(e) and 6(2) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, an intermediary could retain a tank fishery and hold it directly under the State, but the proviso to Section 6(2) applied where the fishery was held under a lease immediately before vesting. Sections 4 and 5 provided for vesting and the consequences for tenants. The Court held that there could be no valid nine-year lease without a registered deed and that an interest confined to catching fish, without rights in the tank’s subsoil or banks, was not a lease of the tank. Relying on Anand Behera v. State of Orissa, the Court noted that a right to catch fish is a profit à prendre in immovable property, accompanied by a licence to enter the land for that purpose.

rule.if: tank_fishery_vesting_case and long_term_tank_lease_claimed and no_registered_lease_document and fishing_rights_only and payment_and_cleaning_required

predicates.tank_fishery_vesting_case: The proceeding concerns who holds a tank fishery after land or estate rights vest in the State.
predicates.long_term_tank_lease_claimed: The State or another claimant asserts that occupants held the tank under a long-term lease immediately before vesting.
predicates.no_registered_lease_document: No registered deed or other documentary instrument evidences the asserted long-term lease.
predicates.fishing_rights_only: The occupants’ interest was limited to fish they caught and did not include the tank’s subsoil or banks.
predicates.payment_and_cleaning_required: The occupants paid for their fishing interest and were required to cleanse or maintain the tank.

issues.definition: When a tank-fishery vesting case involves a claimed long-term tank lease but no registered lease document and only a paid fishing-and-cleaning arrangement without rights in the subsoil or banks, the intermediary becomes the State’s tenant.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate tribunal cannot treat a recorded fishing arrangement as a lease of a tank and thereby revise the recorded rights when the evidence establishes no lease of the tank.
material_facts: The finalized record described the tank as the deity’s debuttar property and also referred to alleged tenants paying rent.
The State sought revision of the record under Section 44(2a), and the Settlement Officer rejected the State’s objection after finding that the alleged occupants had only a right to fish.
The appellate tribunal reversed that decision, treated the occupants as tenants of the tank fishery, and held that they became direct tenants of the State.
The High Court quashed the tribunal’s order, and the Supreme Court agreed that the tribunal had wrongly interpreted the record and assumed jurisdiction to revise its entry.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right to quash the appellate tribunal’s order, and the State’s appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 44(2a) empowered a specially authorized officer, on application or suo motu, to revise a finalized entry in the record-of-rights. The Court held that the tribunal, by wrongly interpreting the record to treat the fishing arrangement as a lease, had assumed the jurisdiction to revise the entry. The substantive distinction between a lease of the tank and a licence to fish was determined under Section 6(2), applying the principles stated in Anand Behera v. State of Orissa.

rule.if: record_revision_appeal and tribunal_treated_record_entry_as_tank_lease and no_registered_lease_document and occupants_had_fishing_rights_only

predicates.record_revision_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from an attempt to revise a finalized land-rights record.
predicates.tribunal_treated_record_entry_as_tank_le: The appellate tribunal relied on a record entry to treat occupants as tenants of the tank fishery.
predicates.no_registered_lease_document: No registered deed or other documentary instrument evidences the asserted lease of the tank.
predicates.occupants_had_fishing_rights_only: The occupants’ interest was limited to catching fish and did not include rights in the tank’s subsoil or banks.

issues.definition: When an appellate tribunal in a record-revision appeal treats a record entry as establishing a tank lease despite the absence of a registered lease document and evidence of fishing rights only, its order is quashed.
